title: Small to Big Converter
context: Grade 5, the pages on changing a smaller unit of time into a bigger one. An adult sees a long division with a remainder. What the pages are doing is making the quotient count the bigger unit and the remainder stay in the smaller unit, so the answer has two parts, and making the part left over always fewer than one of the bigger unit.

writeup.why: Change hours into days, minutes into hours and seconds into minutes by dividing by 24 or 60 and keeping the remainder in the smaller unit, and regroup a leftover part that is too big.
writeup.look: A unit ladder of four rungs, a tray of deep blue blocks, a Group button that sweeps them into piles, and a bundle for a leftover part that is too big.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Small to Big Converter' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of piles made. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The unit ladder of four rungs, days, hours, minutes and seconds, stands down the left of the area at x 90 from y 230 to y 690, each rung 115 tall, with the unit fact beside each step in violet, labelled Regroup. The tray stands at x 520, y 240, 500 by 260, and the blocks the question gives lie in it in deep blue, labelled Given, in rows of the same length. The Group button stands at x 900, y 230, and each press sweeps the blocks into piles of twenty-four or sixty, each full pile lifting to the next rung up as one bar of the bigger unit. The blocks that cannot fill a pile stay behind in the tray under the smaller rung, amber while the child counts them. The division is written in ink under the ladder along y 620, with its quotient and its remainder, and the answer is read in green, labelled Answer, at x 520, y 680 as the bigger unit and the smaller unit together. On the fourth phase the Bundle button stands at x 900, y 330 and wraps 60 of the leftover minutes into a violet tile, labelled Carry, that is dragged to the hours column. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a delete key, and keys for days, h, min and s. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the nine tools of this chapter share them. What the question gives, as a clock time, a length of time, a start date or a number of days, is deep blue, labelled Given or Start. What the working reaches, as an end time, a length of time, a converted time or a date, is green, labelled Answer, End or How long. The thin second hand and the seconds it counts are vermilion, labelled Second hand. One jump along a time line, and one regrouped unit carried or borrowed, are violet, labelled Jump, Carry or Regroup. On a day bar the half from noon until just before midnight is rose, labelled p.m., and the half from midnight until just before noon stays warm white inside its outline, labelled a.m. The hand, digit, column, jump or date being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open, labelled Place holder, and for nothing else. The hour hand and the minute hand, dials, tick marks, time lines, arrows, operation signs and step labels are near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength. Chrome never borrows one of the content colours, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The last tray stays on the stage with its piles lifted to the bigger rung, the blocks left over in the smaller rung and the answer beside them in green.

phases.win: the days and the leftover hours are read together and turn green
phases.does: presses Group to sweep the hour blocks into piles of twenty-four, lifts each full pile to the days rung, and counts the blocks left over
phases.goal: 1 day is 24 h, so divide the hours by 24; the quotient counts days and the remainder stays in hours
phases.says: How many hours fill one day? What is left over?
phases.check: Away from the screen: if some blocks are left over, which unit are they counted in?
phases.feels: the blocks sweeping into piles, the piles lifting, and a few blocks staying behind
phases.hands: Count out counters on a desk and push them into heaps of twenty-four, one heap for each day. Count the heaps, then look at the counters that are left.
phases.tries: First rung: group just one day's worth of blocks and count what is left. Second rung: group two days' worth with a few over. Third rung: the same task with exactly enough blocks and none over, before the question's own blocks return.

wrong.why: the days are the big number, and the few leftover hours look like nothing
wrong.move: gives the quotient with no remainder, so the leftover hours vanish
wrong.screen: the answer stays in the slot, the blocks left in the tray are lit amber under the hours rung, and they are counted in ink as hours

wrong.why: ten was the number for changing units in the last chapter, and the habit carries over
wrong.move: divides by ten, as on the chart of metric units
wrong.screen: the blocks are swept again with twenty-four in each pile, and the child's piles are laid beside them, far too many

phases.screen: a tray of hour blocks in deep blue, and the ladder with its days rung empty

phases.goal: 1 h is 60 min, so divide the minutes by 60; the quotient counts hours and the remainder stays in minutes
phases.says: Sixty minutes fill an hour. How many piles, and what is left?
phases.check: Away from the screen: multiply the hours by sixty and add the minutes left over. Do you get back to where you began?
phases.feels: piles of sixty lifting to the hours rung one after another
phases.hands: Lay minute cards in a row and sweep them into piles of sixty. Lift each pile to a card marked for one hour, and keep the minute cards that are left in a small heap.
phases.tries: First rung: sweep just one hour's worth of minute blocks and count what is left. Second rung: sweep two hours' worth with some over. Third rung: the same task with a heap that needs many piles, before the question's own blocks return.

wrong.why: a number of hundreds looks as if it should be shared into hundreds
wrong.move: divides by a hundred because the number has three digits
wrong.screen: the blocks are swept again with sixty in each pile, and the child's piles are laid beside them, far too few

phases.screen: a tray of minute blocks in deep blue, and the ladder with its hours rung empty
phases.soWhat: 1 h is 60 min, so divide the minutes by 60; the quotient counts hours, and the remainder stays in minutes

phases.win: the minutes and the leftover seconds are read together and turn green
phases.does: sweeps the second blocks into piles of sixty, lifts each full pile to the minutes rung, and counts the blocks left over
phases.goal: 1 min is 60 s, so divide the seconds by 60; the quotient counts minutes and the remainder stays in seconds
phases.says: Sixty seconds fill a minute. Which unit does the leftover part stay in?
phases.check: Away from the screen: why can the seconds left over never make a whole pile?
phases.feels: piles of sixty lifting to the minutes rung and a few seconds left in the tray
phases.hands: Watch the second hand of a real clock go round several times, counting the turns. Then lay out second cards and sweep them into piles of sixty, one pile for each turn.
phases.tries: First rung: sweep a few seconds into one pile and see what is left. Second rung: sweep enough for several piles. Third rung: the same task with a big heap of seconds, before the question's own blocks return.

writeup.delight: On the fourth phase, as the last bundle is wrapped, sixty small blocks fold into one violet tile that slides across to the hours column, and the minutes left over shrink to fewer than sixty.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet grouped. On the first phase a tray of deep blue hour blocks lies in rows of the same length beside the ladder, with its days rung empty. On the second the tray holds minute blocks and the hours rung is empty, and on the third it holds second blocks and the minutes rung is empty. On the fourth a length in hours and minutes stands in deep blue with more than sixty minutes in it. One thing moves, once: the Group button or the full pile among the minutes gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.
writeup.freePlay: Any number of blocks set in the tray and grouped into piles of any size, and any leftover part bundled and carried. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on hours into days, minutes into hours, seconds into minutes and a leftover part that is too big.
voiceLines: A tray of blocks, waiting to be swept into piles.
How many hours fill one day? What is left over?
Sixty minutes fill an hour. How many piles, and what is left?
Sixty seconds fill a minute. Which unit does the leftover part stay in?
Are there a whole sixty minutes in the leftover part? Bundle them and carry.
A new tray of blocks. Sweep it into piles the same way.
Free play. Put any blocks in the tray and group them as you like.
Count the blocks left in the tray again. Do they fill a pile?
You grouped a smaller unit into a bigger one and kept the remainder.

observations.why: a pile holds exactly as many blocks as make one of the bigger unit.
observations.soWhat: the number of piles is the number of the bigger unit.
observations.observe: Every full pile of blocks lifted to the bigger rung as one bar.

observations.why: they are fewer than one of the bigger unit.
observations.soWhat: the remainder stays in the smaller unit, so the answer has two parts.
observations.observe: The blocks that could not fill a pile stayed in the tray under the smaller rung.

observations.why: 100 divided by 24 is 4, remainder 4, and that is not one number of days and hours.
observations.soWhat: say the division and its remainder first, then read the answer, and check by multiplying back and adding the remainder.
observations.observe: The division was written with its remainder, and the answer was read after it.

observations.why: 60 min make 1 h, so a leftover part of that size holds a whole hour it has not yet made.
observations.soWhat: the part left over is always fewer than one of the bigger unit.
observations.observe: A leftover part of more than sixty minutes was bundled and carried to the hours.

serves.exercise: converting four lengths of time in hours into days and hours
converting four lengths of time in minutes into hours and minutes
converting four lengths of time in seconds into minutes and seconds

source_tool.description: The unit ladder of four rungs, days, hours, minutes and seconds, stands down the left of the working area, with the unit fact beside each step in violet, labelled Regroup. The number of the smaller unit the question gives is set in the tray as deep blue blocks, labelled Given, in rows that are easy to count. A Group button sweeps the blocks into piles of twenty-four or sixty, and each full pile lifts to the next rung up as one bar of the bigger unit. The blocks that cannot fill a pile stay behind in the tray under the smaller rung, amber while the child counts them. The division is written under the ladder with its quotient and its remainder, and the answer is read in green, labelled Answer, as the bigger unit and the smaller unit together. On the last phase a length in hours and minutes whose minutes are 60 or more shows a full pile among its minutes; the child bundles it and carries it to the hours as a violet tile, labelled Carry. The running count at the top left of the canvas counts the piles made.
source_tool.art_direction: Counters swept into piles on a table / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: round clock faces with twelve numbers and sixty small marks, a day bar from midnight to midnight, a time line with jumps, columns of hours, minutes and seconds, and month calendars with seven columns.

Every clock time is written in one notation: 4:15 p.m. for a 12-hour time, with a colon and a.m. or p.m., and 1615 hours for a 24-hour time, four digits and the word hours, never a colon and never a dot. Noon is written 12 noon and midnight 12 midnight. A length of time is written 2 h 15 min, 3 days 5 h and 40 s, or in words, and never as a clock time.

Every hour hand sits at its true angle: it moves on from each number as the minutes pass, so at a quarter past it has gone a quarter of the way to the next number. The minute hand is long, the hour hand short and thick, and the second hand thin, longer than both and vermilion. Label lines stay outside the dial.
A time line that passes 12 midnight shows midnight as its own mark and says the next day after it. A count of days always says whether both the first and the last day are counted.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: hands turning, a jump along a time line, a carried unit moving to the next column, or dates being counted on a calendar.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a hand, a digit, a jump or a date the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a time plays in a piece of working: what the question gives, a clock time, a length of time, a start date or a number of days, is deep blue, and what the working reaches, an end time, a length of time, a converted time or a date, is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The thin second hand and the seconds it counts are vermilion. One jump along a time line, and one regrouped unit carried or borrowed, is violet. The half of the day from noon until just before midnight is rose on a day bar, and the half from midnight until just before noon stays warm white inside its outline. The hand, digit, column, jump or date being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open at the front of a 24-hour time. The hour hand and the minute hand are near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Second hand, Jump, Carry, a.m., p.m., Noon and Midnight, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Count the blocks left in the tray again. Do they fill a pile?
voice.onNext: A new tray of blocks. Sweep it into piles the same way.
voice.opening: A tray of blocks, waiting to be swept into piles.
voice.onFinish: You grouped a smaller unit into a bigger one and kept the remainder.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Put any blocks in the tray and group them as you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has shared a heap of counters into equal groups by hand and said what is left over. The tool is what sweeps the blocks into piles of 24 or 60 and lifts each pile to the next unit, which a long division on paper only shows as figures.

answer_key.rule: To change a smaller unit into a bigger one, divide. 1 day is 24 h, 1 h is 60 min and 1 min is 60 s. The quotient counts the bigger unit and the remainder stays in the smaller unit: 77 divided by 24 is 3, remainder 5, so 77 h is 3 days 5 h. The check is to multiply back and add the remainder. A leftover part of 60 or more is regrouped: 75 min is 1 h 15 min, so 5 h 75 min is 6 h 15 min. The part left over is always fewer than one of the bigger unit.
answer_key.wrong: The stage keeps the child's piles. A pile made with the wrong number of blocks stays, and the number that the unit needs is lit amber beside it. A remainder counted as part of the quotient stays in the bigger unit's row, lit amber. A leftover part that is still 60 or more shows the full pile it has not made yet, lit amber. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: 1 day is 24 h, so divide the hours by 24.
The 6 counts whole days, and the remainder 6 counts hours.
items.question: How many days and hours are there in 150 h?
items.checkpoint: Divide by 24 for days: the quotient counts days, and the remainder stays in hours.
items.misconception: Giving the quotient with no remainder, so the leftover hours vanish and only the days are said.

steps: 1 h is 60 min, so divide the minutes by 60.
The 6 counts whole hours, and the remainder 35 counts minutes.
Check it: 6 x 60 + 35 = 395. So 395 min is 6 h 35 min.
items.question: How many hours and minutes are there in 395 min?
items.checkpoint: Divide by 60 for hours: the quotient counts hours, and the remainder stays in minutes.
items.misconception: Dividing by 100 because the number has three digits, when an hour is 60 min and not 100.

steps: 1 min is 60 s, so divide the seconds by 60.
The 12 counts whole minutes, and the remainder 5 counts seconds.
items.question: How many minutes and seconds are there in 725 s?
items.checkpoint: Divide by 60 for minutes: the quotient counts minutes, and the remainder stays in seconds.
items.misconception: Writing the remainder as a decimal part of a minute, when it is a whole number of seconds.

steps: 70 min is more than 1 h, so the leftover part is too big.
70 min is 1 h 10 min, so carry the 1 h to the hours.
6 + 1 = 7, so the hours are 7 and the minutes left are 10.
Check it: 7 x 60 + 10 = 430, and 6 x 60 + 70 = 430. So 6 h 70 min is 7 h 10 min.
items.question: Write 6 h 70 min in the best way.
items.checkpoint: A leftover part of 60 or more is regrouped as one of the bigger unit, so the minutes left are fewer than 60.
items.misconception: Leaving 70 min as it stands, because the numbers are right, when the minutes should be fewer than 60.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: How many days and hours are there in 55 h?
items.final_answer: 2 days 7 h, because 55 divided by 24 is 2, remainder 7

items.question: How many hours and minutes are there in 130 min?
items.final_answer: 2 h 10 min, because 130 divided by 60 is 2, remainder 10

items.question: How many minutes and seconds are there in 190 s?
items.final_answer: 3 min 10 s, because 190 divided by 60 is 3, remainder 10

items.question: Write 4 h 75 min in the best way.
items.final_answer: 5 h 15 min, because 75 min is 1 h 15 min

items.question: How many days and hours are there in 290 h?
items.final_answer: 12 days 2 h, because 290 divided by 24 is 12, remainder 2

items.question: How many hours and minutes are there in 470 min?
items.final_answer: 7 h 50 min, because 470 divided by 60 is 7, remainder 50

items.question: How many minutes and seconds are there in 2000 s?
items.final_answer: 33 min 20 s, because 2000 divided by 60 is 33, remainder 20

items.question: Write 2 h 200 min in the best way.
items.final_answer: 5 h 20 min, because 200 min is 3 h 20 min

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: sweeps the blocks in the tray into piles of 24 or 60
lifts a full pile to the next rung of the ladder
wraps 60 of a leftover part into a carry tile
is dragged to the bigger unit's column
types a quotient, a remainder or an answer

teaching_notes: Say the unit fact aloud before every conversion. Divide by 24 for days and by 60 for hours or minutes, and say which unit the quotient counts. The remainder stays in the smaller unit, so say the word remainder and then read the answer. Write a division as a division with its remainder, and the answer after it, never as if the division were equal to an answer in two units. Check by multiplying back and adding the remainder. The part left over is always fewer than one of the bigger unit.
generation_prompt: Build a unit conversion tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A unit ladder of four rungs, days, hours, minutes and seconds, stands on the left with the unit fact beside each step in violet, labelled Regroup. The number of the smaller unit the question gives is set in a tray as deep blue blocks, labelled Given. A Group button sweeps them into piles of twenty-four or sixty, each full pile lifts to the next rung as one bar of the bigger unit, and the blocks that cannot fill a pile stay behind, amber while counted. The division is written under the ladder with its quotient and its remainder, and the answer is read in green, labelled Answer. On the last phase a leftover part of 60 or more is bundled and carried to the bigger unit as a violet tile, labelled Carry. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Set the blocks in the tray. Group them into piles of 24 or 60, lift each full pile up, and read the bigger unit and the blocks left over.
